texts.preamble: K. Rama Mohan Rao, vs The State Of Andhra Pradesh, on 30 August, 2018 Smt Justice T. Rajani Criminal Petition No.4609 of 2011 Order:
texts.facts: The criminal petition is filed for quash of the proceedings in CC.No.260 of 2007 on the file of the Judicial First Class Magistrate, Sathupally, Khammam District, registered for the offence under Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The facts of the case are that the sample taken up herein is Dalda Vanaspathi and it was lifted on 23.02.2006 and sent for analysis on 24.02.2006 and the report was received on 01.04.2006 and permission for the complaint was granted on 04.12.2006 and proceedings were initiated on 26.02.2007.
texts.arguments: 4. The main contention of the counsel for the petitioner is that by the date of complaint itself, the shelf life of Dalda Vanaspathi is over, it being six months. The counsel expressed that there is prejudice caused to the petitioner and that by virtue of the delay in filing the report, the opportunity provided under Section 13(2) of the Act to send a sample for second analysis is lost. Learned counsel also relies on the order in CRLP.No.829 of 2003 dated 01.03.20064 wherein the Court by considering the similar submissions and taking into consideration the inordinate delay, not only in issuing notice, but 2 TR, J also in launching prosecution against the accused, [LEAKAGE_MASK] the further proceedings. 5. 7. This Court in R. HARI HARA REDDY v. STATE OF ANDHRA PRADESH1 wherein it was held that the inordinate delay in filing the complaint would deprive the valuable right offered on the K. The decision of the Supreme Court in STATE OF HARYANA v. UNIQUE FARMAID (P) LTD.2 is also on the same lines. The contention therein that in the absence of the statutory time limit the shelf life of the sample was not relevant, was rejected. Relevant portion at paragraphs 11 and 12 observed as follows: "11. Sub-section (1) of Section 30 which appears to be relevant only prescribes in effect that ignorance would be of no defence but that does not mean that if there are contraventions of other mandatory provisions of the Act, the accused have no remedy. In State of Punjab v. National Organic Chemical Industries Ltd. [(1996) 11 SCC 613] this Court in somewhat similar circumstances said that the procedure laid down under Section 24 of the Act deprived the accused to have sample tested by the Central Insecticides Laboratory and adduce evidence of the report so given in his defence. In this connection reference be made to decisions of this Court in State of Haryana v. Brij Lal Mittal [(1998) 5 SCC 343] under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940; Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Ghisa Ram [AIR 1967 SC 970]; Chetumal v. State of Madhya Pradesh & Anr. [(1981) 3 SCC 72} and Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf, [(1999)] 2 SCC 400] all under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. Under sub-section (3) of Section 24 report signed by the Insecticide analyst shall be evidence of the facts stated therein and shall be conclusive evidence against the accused only if the accused do not, within 28 days of the receipt of the report, notify in writing to the Insecticides Inspector or the Court before which proceedings are pending that they K.
